questions.questionText: What are the five events in Scrum?

options.text: Sprint Planning, Daily Standup, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective, and Backlog Refinement
Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective
Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective, and Release Planning
Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Standup, Backlog Grooming, and Sprint Review

explanation.correct: The five Scrum events are: Sprint (the container), Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective. Backlog refinement is NOT a Scrum event.
explanation.incorrect: Backlog refinement and release planning are not Scrum events. 'Daily Standup' is informal â€” the correct Scrum term is 'Daily Scrum'.
explanation.examTip: 5 Scrum events: Sprint (container for all others), Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Retrospective. Refinement is NOT one of the 5.

questions.questionText: What is the maximum length of a Sprint in Scrum?

options.text: 2 weeks
4 weeks (1 calendar month)
6 weeks
There is no maximum â€” it depends on the team's needs

explanation.correct: The Scrum Guide specifies a maximum Sprint length of one calendar month (4 weeks). Shorter sprints reduce risk and provide more frequent opportunities to inspect and adapt.
explanation.incorrect: 2 weeks is common but not the maximum. Sprints longer than a month are not Scrum. The maximum is explicitly defined as one month.
explanation.examTip: Sprint length: 1 week to 1 month. Must be consistent (same length each sprint). Shorter = less risk. Max = 1 calendar month.

questions.questionText: What is the Sprint Goal?

options.text: The list of Product Backlog items selected for the sprint
A single objective that provides focus and flexibility to the Developers during the sprint
The target velocity the team aims to achieve
The deadline by which the sprint must be completed

explanation.correct: The Sprint Goal is the single objective for the sprint, created during Sprint Planning. It provides coherence and focus, and gives the Developers flexibility in how to achieve it.
explanation.incorrect: The Sprint Backlog contains selected items. Velocity is a metric. Sprint deadline = the sprint end date.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Goal: created in Sprint Planning, committed to by Developers, gives flexibility in implementation. If Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, the PO can cancel the sprint.

questions.questionText: What is the timebox for the Daily Scrum?

options.text: 30 minutes
15 minutes
As long as needed to resolve all issues
1 hour

explanation.correct: The Daily Scrum is time-boxed to 15 minutes. It is held at the same time and place every working day to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation.incorrect: 30 minutes and 1 hour are too long. The Daily Scrum should not be extended to resolve all issues â€” longer discussions happen after.
explanation.examTip: Daily Scrum: 15 min timebox, same time, same place, for Developers. SM may facilitate but Developers run it. Issues raised in Daily Scrum are resolved AFTER the event.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?

options.text: To report individual progress to the Scrum Master and Product Owner
To inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog as necessary
To identify and resolve all impediments blocking the team
To update the burndown chart and velocity metrics

explanation.correct: The Daily Scrum's purpose is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog â€” planning work for the next 24 hours to optimise their chance of meeting the Sprint Goal.
explanation.incorrect: It's not a status report to management or leadership. Impediments are noted but resolved after. Charts and metrics are not the focus.
explanation.examTip: Daily Scrum is FOR Developers, BY Developers. The SM can facilitate but doesn't need to attend. PO doesn't need to attend. It's not a status meeting.

questions.questionText: What is the timebox for Sprint Planning for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: 2 hours
4 hours
8 hours
As long as needed to plan all the work

explanation.correct: Sprint Planning is time-boxed to a maximum of 8 hours for a one-month Sprint. For shorter sprints, the event is usually shorter proportionally.
explanation.incorrect: 2 and 4 hours are for shorter sprints. Sprint Planning has an explicit maximum â€” it doesn't go as long as needed.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Planning timebox: max 8h for 1-month sprint. Proportionally shorter for shorter sprints (4h for 2-week, 2h for 1-week). All Scrum events are time-boxed.

questions.questionText: What are the three topics addressed during Sprint Planning?

options.text: What to build, how to build it, and who will build it
Why is the sprint valuable, what can be done, and how will the work get done
Sprint Goal, acceptance criteria, and task assignments
Velocity, capacity, and backlog ordering

explanation.correct: Sprint Planning addresses three topics: Why (Sprint Goal â€” why is this sprint valuable?), What (which Product Backlog items to select), and How (how will Developers create a Done Increment?).
explanation.incorrect: Task assignments don't happen in Sprint Planning. Velocity and backlog ordering are inputs, not topics.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Planning 3 topics: WHY (Sprint Goal), WHAT (selected PBIs), HOW (how to create the Increment). The 2020 Scrum Guide added WHY as explicit first topic.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Sprint Review?

options.text: To evaluate the team's process and identify improvements for next sprint
To inspect the Increment and adapt the Product Backlog based on stakeholder feedback
To formally accept completed user stories as done
To measure the team's velocity and update metrics

explanation.correct: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome of the sprint (the Increment) and adapts the Product Backlog. It is a collaborative working session with stakeholders to review what was built and discuss what to do next.
explanation.incorrect: Process evaluation = Sprint Retrospective. Formal story acceptance is not a Scrum concept. Velocity tracking is not the purpose.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Review = what we built (inspect Increment). Sprint Retrospective = how we worked (improve process). Never confuse the two.

questions.questionText: What is the timebox for the Sprint Review for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: 2 hours
3 hours
4 hours
1 hour per week of sprint length

explanation.correct: The Sprint Review is time-boxed to a maximum of 4 hours for a one-month Sprint. Shorter sprints have proportionally shorter reviews.
explanation.incorrect: The timebox is 4 hours maximum for a 1-month sprint. Proportionally shorter for shorter sprints.
explanation.examTip: Scrum event timeboxes (1-month sprint): Planning 8h, Daily Scrum 15min, Sprint Review 4h, Retrospective 3h. Sprint itself = max 1 month.

questions.questionText: What is the purpose of the Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: To demonstrate completed work to stakeholders
To plan work for the next sprint
To inspect how the last sprint went and create a plan for improvements
To review the Product Backlog and reprioritise items

explanation.correct: The Sprint Retrospective inspects the last sprint regarding people, relationships, processes, and tools â€” and identifies the most impactful improvements to implement in the next sprint.
explanation.incorrect: Demonstrating work = Sprint Review. Planning next sprint = Sprint Planning. Reprioritising backlog = ongoing PO activity.
explanation.examTip: Retro output = at least one improvement to implement next sprint (it goes into the Sprint Backlog). If no improvements are acted on, the Retro has no value.

questions.questionText: What is the timebox for the Sprint Retrospective for a one-month Sprint?

options.text: 1 hour
2 hours
3 hours
4 hours

explanation.correct: The Sprint Retrospective is time-boxed to a maximum of 3 hours for a one-month Sprint â€” shorter for shorter sprints.
explanation.incorrect: 4 hours is the Sprint Review timebox. 3 hours is for the Retrospective.
explanation.examTip: Event timeboxes: Planning (8h), Daily Scrum (15min), Review (4h), Retrospective (3h). Note: Retro is shorter than Review.

questions.scenarioText: During a Sprint Retrospective, the team identifies that poor test environment stability caused many issues in the last sprint. The Scrum Master suggests adding a task to fix the environment to the Sprint Backlog.
questions.questionText: Is this appropriate, and why?

options.text: No â€” retrospective improvements should only be recorded in a separate improvement backlog
Yes â€” the highest priority improvements identified in the Retrospective may be added to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint
No â€” the Scrum Master cannot add items to the Sprint Backlog
Yes â€” but only if the Product Owner approves the improvement

explanation.correct: The Scrum Guide states that the Scrum Team identifies the most impactful improvements from the Retrospective and adds them to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint â€” ensuring process improvements actually get done.
explanation.incorrect: A separate improvement backlog is one approach but Scrum Guide says Sprint Backlog. SM alone doesn't add (team decides). PO approval not required for process improvements.
explanation.examTip: Retro improvements â†’ Sprint Backlog (at least one). This ensures improvements are actually acted on, not just discussed. Process improvements are the team's responsibility.

questions.questionText: When can a Sprint be cancelled in Scrum?

options.text: When the team falls significantly behind their velocity targets
Only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete, and only by the Product Owner
When the Scrum Master determines the team is not working effectively
At any time if a majority of Developers agree it is necessary

explanation.correct: Only the Product Owner has authority to cancel a Sprint, and only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete (e.g., market conditions change, technology becomes unavailable). Sprint cancellations are very rare.
explanation.incorrect: Velocity is not a cancellation criterion. SM cannot cancel. Developers cannot cancel. Only PO, only when Sprint Goal is obsolete.
explanation.examTip: Sprint cancellation: PO only, Sprint Goal obsolete only. Rare and disruptive. All completed Done work is reviewed, incomplete work returned to Product Backlog.

questions.questionText: Place the Scrum events in the order they occur within a Sprint.

explanation.correct: Within a Sprint: Sprint Planning (start) â†’ Daily Scrum (every day) â†’ Sprint Review (end, stakeholders) â†’ Sprint Retrospective (last event). Then the next Sprint begins.
explanation.incorrect: The Retrospective always comes AFTER the Review â€” process improvement happens after inspecting the product.
explanation.examTip: Sprint sequence: Planning â†’ [daily work + Daily Scrum] â†’ Review â†’ Retrospective â†’ next Sprint Planning. Retro is the last event before a new sprint starts.

questions.questionText: What is the output of Sprint Planning?

options.text: An updated Product Backlog and a list of sprint tasks
A Sprint Backlog that includes the Sprint Goal, selected PBIs, and a plan for delivery
A commitment from the team to complete all selected stories
A detailed project plan for the entire sprint duration

explanation.correct: Sprint Planning's output is the Sprint Backlog: the Sprint Goal (why), the selected PBIs (what), and the plan for delivering the Increment (how). The Sprint Backlog also includes at least one improvement from the Retrospective.
explanation.incorrect: The Product Backlog is updated by PO, not Sprint Planning. The team commits to the Sprint Goal, not necessarily completing every story. Detailed project plans are waterfall, not Scrum.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Backlog = Sprint Goal + selected PBIs + plan. The plan evolves daily. Developers commit to the Sprint Goal, not a story count.

questions.questionText: Who is accountable for creating the Sprint Goal?

options.text: The Product Owner alone
The Scrum Team collaboratively during Sprint Planning
The Developers alone
The Scrum Master, who ensures it aligns with business objectives

explanation.correct: The Sprint Goal is created collaboratively by the entire Scrum Team during Sprint Planning. The whole team crafts it â€” although the Product Owner proposes the objective and the Developers commit to the goal.
explanation.incorrect: While PO has strong input (they understand value), the Sprint Goal is a collaborative Scrum Team creation. The SM doesn't set the goal.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Goal created by: whole Scrum Team in Sprint Planning. PO proposes the 'why' (value). Devs discuss feasibility and commit to it. Collaborative creation.

questions.questionText: Can the Daily Scrum format be changed from the classic three-question format?

options.text: No â€” the Scrum Guide mandates the three questions: what did I do yesterday, what will I do today, and any blockers
Yes â€” the Developers can use any structure they find useful as long as the event focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal
Yes â€” but only with the Scrum Master's approval
No â€” the format is prescribed by the Scrum Master

explanation.correct: The 2020 Scrum Guide removed the three-question format. Developers can use any structure they choose, as long as the Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and results in a plan for the next day.
explanation.incorrect: The three questions were a suggested format in earlier versions â€” the 2020 guide removed this prescription. SM doesn't approve the format.
explanation.examTip: 2020 Scrum Guide change: Daily Scrum no longer mandates the three questions. Developers choose their own format. Focus = Sprint Goal progress.

questions.questionText: For each statement, indicate whether it correctly describes Scrum events.

statements.text: The Sprint Review is a demo where the team presents completed work to stakeholders.
The Sprint Retrospective inspects people, relationships, processes, and tools.
All Scrum events have fixed timeboxes that cannot be shortened.
Sprint Planning results in both a Sprint Goal and a Sprint Backlog.

explanation.correct: Sprint Review = collaborative working session (not just a demo). Retrospective inspects people/relationships/processes/tools. Timeboxes are maximums â€” events can end early. Sprint Planning outputs both Sprint Goal and Sprint Backlog.
explanation.incorrect: Sprint Review is more than a demo â€” it's an adaptation event for the Product Backlog. Timeboxes are maximums, not minimums.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Review â‰  demo. It's a collaborative inspection of the Increment and adaptation of the Product Backlog. Stakeholders participate actively.

questions.questionText: Who facilitates the Sprint Planning?

options.text: The Product Owner â€” they know the backlog best
The Scrum Master facilitates and ensures the event occurs and is productive within the timebox
The most senior Developer
An external project manager or Agile coach

explanation.correct: The Scrum Master facilitates Scrum events â€” they ensure events occur, are time-boxed, and are productive. For Sprint Planning, the SM facilitates while the whole team participates.
explanation.incorrect: PO contributes to Sprint Planning but doesn't facilitate it. Senior Developers can help but SM facilitates. External facilitators are not prescribed.
explanation.examTip: SM facilitates all Scrum events. But facilitation means ensuring the event is productive â€” not running it solo. All team members participate actively.

questions.questionText: What is the main output of the Sprint Review?

options.text: A list of improvements the team will make in the next sprint
A revised Product Backlog reflecting what to do next based on stakeholder feedback
A formal sign-off document that stories are accepted
An updated Sprint Backlog for the next sprint

explanation.correct: The Sprint Review's primary output is a revised Product Backlog â€” updated by the PO based on the collaborative discussion and stakeholder feedback during the review.
explanation.incorrect: Process improvements = Retrospective output. Formal sign-offs are not Scrum. Sprint Backlog is created in Sprint Planning, not Sprint Review.
explanation.examTip: Sprint Review outputs: revised Product Backlog (what to do next), insights from stakeholders, feedback on Increment. Not: process improvements (that's the Retro).

questions.questionText: What happens if the Scrum Team skips the Sprint Retrospective?

options.text: Nothing â€” Retrospectives are optional if the team is performing well
The team loses a formal opportunity to inspect their process and adapt â€” leading to persistent problems and slower improvement
The Scrum Master receives a formal warning from the organisation
The sprint is invalid and must be restarted

explanation.correct: Skipping the Retrospective removes the team's formal adaptation event for process improvement. Problems accumulate without a structured space to address them. The Retrospective is a mandatory Scrum event.
explanation.incorrect: Retrospectives are not optional â€” they are one of the 5 Scrum events. No formal warning mechanism in Scrum. Skipping doesn't invalidate the sprint.
explanation.examTip: All 5 Scrum events are mandatory. Skipping any event weakens empiricism. 'We're doing well' is not a reason to skip the Retro â€” continuous improvement is always possible.

questions.questionText: At what point during the Sprint should the Sprint Retrospective occur?

options.text: At the beginning of the sprint before Sprint Planning
After the Sprint Review and before the next Sprint Planning
At the midpoint of the sprint to allow time to implement improvements
At any time during the sprint at the team's discretion

explanation.correct: The Sprint Retrospective occurs after the Sprint Review (inspect what was built) and before the next Sprint Planning (begin new sprint). It's the last event before the next sprint begins.
explanation.incorrect: Retro is at the end of the sprint, not the beginning, middle, or ad-hoc.
explanation.examTip: Sprint event order: Sprint Planning â†’ Daily Scrum (during) â†’ Sprint Review â†’ Sprint Retrospective â†’ next Sprint Planning. Retro is always the final event.

questions.questionText: Is the Product Owner required to attend the Daily Scrum?

options.text: Yes â€” the PO must attend to provide daily backlog updates
No â€” the Daily Scrum is for Developers. The PO attends only if they are also doing development work
Yes â€” the PO attends to track sprint progress
No â€” the PO is banned from the Daily Scrum entirely

explanation.correct: The Daily Scrum is specifically for the Developers. The PO is not required to attend unless they are also contributing as a Developer on the Sprint Backlog. Attending for tracking purposes undermines the event's purpose.
explanation.incorrect: Attending for updates or tracking turns Daily Scrum into a status report, not a team planning session.
explanation.examTip: Daily Scrum attendees = Developers. SM and PO can be present but should not disrupt. If PO attends to 'track', this is a red flag â€” it suggests lack of trust.

questions.questionText: Match each Scrum event to its maximum timebox for a one-month Sprint.

explanation.correct: Sprint Planning = 8h. Sprint Review = 4h. Sprint Retrospective = 3h. Daily Scrum = 15 minutes (always, regardless of sprint length).
explanation.incorrect: Remember: Planning longest (8h), Review shorter (4h), Retro shortest of the longer events (3h), Daily always 15min.
explanation.examTip: Timebox memory: Planning 8h, Review 4h, Retro 3h, Daily 15min. Shorter sprints = proportionally shorter events (except Daily Scrum = always 15min).
